iut_type: End Product (Alinco XE1177), distinguishing DUT-side firmware faults from test-system-side faults during RF PHY testing -- including an internal disagreement about attribution, and the eventual confirmed root cause
customer_question: Our updated firmware still shows the same error as before: 'SA: ERROR: Initialization of signal analyzer: failed.' Is this caused by something in our firmware update, or is something else going on?
question_variants: Should we report this signal-analyzer initialization error to our firmware developer along with the other power-save mode issue?
Why does our reference device pass the same test without this error, but the customer's DUT shows it intermittently?
If a reference DUT never shows the error but the customer's own DUT does after each firmware update, doesn't that suggest the DUT's firmware really is the cause after all?
actual_issue: An intermittent 'signal analyzer initialization failed' error appeared in some test logs alongside the separate, already-identified firmware power-save mode dropout issue. The lab's own test engineer initially disagreed with the consultant's assessment that this was purely a test-system-side fault -- since a reference DUT verification run never produced the error, while the customer's DUT did, after each successive firmware update -- raising a genuine, unresolved internal question of whether the firmware updates themselves were somehow triggering a system-level fault, before the actual root cause was eventually traced to a hardware connector issue on the lab's own test system.
plain_english_explanation: This particular error ('SA: ERROR: Initialization of signal analyzer: failed') occurred during the test system's own instrument initialization sequence, before any DUT-specific test commands were even issued. The lab's engineer initially pushed back on the consultant's system-side-fault conclusion, pointing out that a reference DUT used to verify the InterLab system never produced this error, while Alinco's own DUT did, repeatedly, after each new firmware revision -- seemingly correlating the error with the customer's firmware rather than the test system. The consultant did not dismiss this concern outright, but re-examined the actual log timeline directly: in every instance, the signal analyzer initialization step that failed occurred before any interaction with the DUT at all, meaning there was no log-based evidence the DUT's firmware could have caused it. The consultant also identified a likely confound behind the apparent correlation: RF and RF PHY test runs were being mixed together without being tracked separately across the initial test, retest, and re-retest rounds, and RF PHY test logs don't even include this particular signal-analyzer-initialization step at all -- so the error could only ever appear in RF test logs, making it look firmware-correlated purely by where attention happened to be focused, rather than by genuine causation. Given the evidence was still inconclusive at that point, the consultant explicitly instructed the team not to tell the customer that their firmware updates were causing fatal test-system errors, since that claim wasn't yet substantiated and could derail the firmware vendor's actual debugging effort. The team then escalated the specific log to InterLab (the test system's manufacturer/support channel) for a root-cause opinion, and as a parallel physical remediation step, cleaned the test system's own R&S FSL signal analyzer LAN connection (removing the Ethernet cable from both ends, air-dusting the RJ45 plug and receptacle, and cleaning the gold-plated contact pins with contact cleaner on a lint-free industrial wipe) -- since the InterLab system's instruments are interconnected via GPIB-over-Ethernet, a degraded physical network connection was a plausible hardware-level explanation consistent with an intermittent, DUT-independent fault. This directly addressed the issue going forward, confirming the error had been a hardware connector/contact problem on the lab's own test system all along, unrelated to the customer's firmware.
consultant_answer: That particular error isn't related to your firmware -- it occurs during our test system's own instrument initialization, before any of your DUT's test commands even run. Our own test engineer initially raised a fair concern, since a reference DUT never showed this error while yours did after each firmware update -- but re-checking the actual log timeline confirmed no DUT interaction happens before the failure point, and we also realized RF PHY test logs don't even include this initialization step at all, which explains why it only ever showed up in RF-test-focused runs rather than reflecting your firmware specifically. We're escalating the log to our test system's support channel and have also physically cleaned the affected connector on our own equipment as a likely hardware fix -- we will not be telling you that your firmware updates caused test-system errors, since that wasn't actually substantiated.
decision_logic: When a test log shows an error originating in the test system's own instrument initialization sequence (before any DUT-specific commands are issued), attribute it to the test system rather than the DUT by default -- but when a team member raises a plausible-sounding correlation-based counter-argument (e.g., 'the reference sample never shows it, but the customer's DUT does after every update'), investigate it seriously by re-examining the actual log timeline and checking for confounds (such as two different test types being run without being tracked separately) before either confirming or overriding the original attribution, and avoid communicating an unsubstantiated causal claim to the customer in the meantime.
final_recommendation: When multiple distinct error types appear during an extended troubleshooting effort, explicitly classify each by where in the test sequence it originates (test-system initialization vs. DUT-specific command execution) before deciding what to relay to the customer or their firmware vendor; take internal disagreement about that classification seriously rather than dismissing it, re-verify against the actual log timeline and check for confounds, and escalate ambiguous test-system-side faults to the test system's own support channel while pursuing direct physical remediation (e.g., cleaning a suspect connector) in parallel, rather than letting an unresolved attribution question stall the broader investigation.
risk_if_done_wrong: Relaying an unrelated test-system-side fault to the customer's firmware vendor alongside the genuine firmware power-save issue could have caused the vendor to waste debugging effort investigating a problem in their own firmware that doesn't actually exist, or to lose confidence in the reported firmware issue's validity. Conversely, dismissing the test engineer's correlation-based concern without re-checking the log timeline could have caused the team to overlook a genuine DUT-side interaction effect, had one actually existed.
